provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation: In the original task the input is two size x size panels (orange top, red bottom) separated by a yellow divider row at the centre. The output is green wherever both panels are background (0) at the same position, and background everywhere else. Each output cell is tied to its two panel cells by a pure translation of size+1 along the stacking axis. Translation commutes with every D4 transform, and the rule is symmetric in the two panels. So in visible coordinates the output is simply AND(panelA==bg, panelB==bg), with no flipping needed, whichever panel ends up first. A divider row stays a row under row-reversal and under even rotations, and becomes a column under odd rotations, so the factory picks the split axis from d4 % 2. It emits code that scans rows or columns directly. Colour roles are specialized as constants: palette[0] is background, palette[3] is the fill (green), and palette[4] is the divider (yellow). The divider is located as a full line of the divider colour; if several exist, the one nearest the centre is used. If none is found, the program falls back to splitting the grid into two equal halves, skipping the middle line. This also handles the spurious-full-line case, such as a top row of all orange.
draft_notes.limitations: The program assumes the constructor's domain: two equal panels separated by a single divider line along one axis, with the divider at the centre. Panel pixels are never the divider colour, so in the visible frame a full divider-coloured line can only be the real separator. Demonstrations are not used, because the axis and colour roles are fully determined by d4 and palette. The fixtures are consistent with the uniform rule; no contradictions were found. I have not run any tests.
